title: What is Claude Mythos? And how is if different from Claude Fable?
summary: Mythos and Fable are actually the same model; Fable just has increased security guardrails to prevent bad actors from using it to develop cyberattacks or new bioweapons.
body_markdown:
On April 7, 2026, Claude Mythos Preview was officially announced, but it was apparently too dangerous to release. According to Anthropic, Claude Mythos[represented a unique cybersecurity threat](https://red.anthropic.com/2026/mythos-preview/) (they claimed that "the fallout—for economies, public safety, and national security—could be severe.")


Instead of releasing Mythos to the general public, they spun up Project Glasswing, a cybersecurity initiative that also involved some big-name companies. The idea was that they'd be able to deploy Mythos for defensive cybersecurity purposes[before an open Chinese model developed the same capabilities](https://zapier.com/blog/what-is-deepseek/) and threw the whole web wide open.


Two months later, Anthropic released a guardrailed version of Mythos—called Fable—that was fully available to the public...for about three days. Then the U.S. government told them they needed to[suspend access to all foreign nationals](https://www.anthropic.com/news/fable-mythos-access) , which realistically meant suspending access for everyone. And on June 30,[that suspension was lifted](https://www.anthropic.com/news/redeploying-fable-5) .


Since then, new versions of the models have been released—now Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Fable 5.1 are Anthropic's most capable models. They aren't designed for everyday use but for maximum performance in tasks like software engineering, scientific research, computer vision, and automating knowledge work. As[Anthropic explains it](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-fable-5-mythos-5) , the longer and more complex the tasks, the more capable Mythos and Fable are relative to other models.


As a tech journalist, I've been covering AI and security (separately and together) for well over a decade. My read is that while there's a degree of marketing to Anthropic's claims, Mythos and Fable are the most powerful models ever released. When they were available, they jumped to[the top of almost every leaderboard](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/claude-fable-5-mythos-intelligence-index) , including Zapier's[AutomationBench](https://zapier.com/benchmarks) , which tests models on real-world workflows.

## What are Claude Mythos and Claude Fable?


Claude Mythos 5.1 and Fable 5.1 are general purpose[large language models (LLM)](https://zapier.com/blog/best-llm/) that are particularly good at coding, reasoning, and vision-based tasks. The only meaningful difference between them is that Fable 5.1 has guardrails that prevent it from answering queries about cybersecurity, chemistry and biology, and distillation ([or how it works](https://www.anthropic.com/news/detecting-and-preventing-distillation-attacks) , in an attempt to train cheaper models). Anthropic estimates that the guardrails kick in in around 5 percent of queries, and in those cases, it automatically falls back to Opus 5.


Mythos has been available since April 7, 2026. At the time, Anthropic claimed it was[too dangerous for wide release](https://red.anthropic.com/2026/mythos-preview/) because it had already uncovered "thousands of high-severity vulnerabilities, including some in every major operating system and web browser."


That's why Mythos Preview was released to Project Glasswing partners. At the time, that included Amazon, Apple, Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, JPMorganChase, the Linux Foundation, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Palo Alto Networks—though[that group has now been expanded](https://www.anthropic.com/news/expanding-project-glasswing) as part of a wider rollout. Initial results suggest the project has been a big success.[Partners found and patched](https://www.anthropic.com/research/glasswing-initial-update) more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity security bugs as a result. While things didn't go full Skynet, it seems like Anthropic's slow rollout was the right approach.


Anthropic also planned to release a version with the biology and chemistry safeguards removed to scientists as part of a trusted access program in the coming months, but we'll see how that pans out given the past suspension.


Incidentally, in launching Mythos 5 and Fable 5 (the first numbered versions of the two models), Anthropic has made a complete mess of its model numbering convention. Its other three models are currently Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and Haiku 4.5. It's still better than what OpenAI is doing, but as someone who has to keep track of these things, it's deeply upsetting.


## How good is Claude Fable 5.1?


There are two ways of looking at how good Claude Fable 5.1 is:


-


The benchmarks and claimed abilities


-


What it's like for real-world applications


First, the benchmarks:[Fable smashes them](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/claude-fable-5-1) —5.1 took the number one spot on Artificial Analysis.


But it also took the lead on Zapier's[AutomationBench](https://zapier.com/benchmarks) , which tests AI models on end-to-end workflow execution using 47 real tools across six business functions. Each task drops an agent into an isolated environment (CRM records, inbox threads, calendars, and more) with the kind of ambiguity that makes real work hard. That's solid evidence that Fable translates into the real world.


**Did you know?** Every time a new major AI model is released, Zapier runs it through[AutomationBench](https://zapier.com/benchmarks) , an open benchmark that tests models on real business workflows.


## How dangerous is Claude Mythos?


[In an article that coincided](https://red.anthropic.com/2026/mythos-preview/) with the launch of Glasswing, cybersecurity researchers at Anthropic detailed Mythos's cybersecurity capabilities.


As I said, I've been[writing about this stuff for years](https://www.popsci.com/authors/harry-guinness/) , and their summary seems legitimately concerning. In some of the worst exploits, under the right circumstances, a hacker could use Mythos to go from an unauthenticated visitor on a website to having admin access on the server.


The big takeaways are that Mythos sounds to be very good at finding and exploiting subtle vulnerabilities. It's also able to combine multiple vulnerabilities into more powerful exploits. In testing, it's found "zero-day" (or undiscovered) exploits in every major operating system and web browser that have been sitting there unfixed for years. The oldest bug it found was from the '90s in OpenBSD.


Mythos is significantly better at this than Opus 4.8 or Sonnet 5. The researchers go into a deep technical explanation of some of the exploits Mythos found, and it's worth reading if you're technically inclined.


Image source:[Anthropic](https://red.anthropic.com/2026/mythos-preview/)


The researchers stress that Mythos wasn't trained to have these capabilities. They emerged as an unintended consequence of its improvements in coding, reasoning, and autonomy. It's better at finding and fixing vulnerabilities too, but it's now good enough to exploit them as well.


While this information comes from Mythos Preview rather than Mythos 5.1, it's safe to assume its capabilities are only improving. The[early project Glasswing results](https://www.anthropic.com/research/glasswing-initial-update) also back them up, with partners finding more than 10,000 serious security bugs in its first few weeks.


I'm not a biochemist, so I can't assess whether the fears about Mythos being used to develop novel viruses and biochemical weapons are overblown, but AI models have shown a huge amount of promise with drug development, protein folding, and other adjacent fields, so I wouldn't rule it out. There's also the fear that by lowering the barrier for entry, they'd essentially enable bad actors to vibe-compound dangerous chemicals.


I don't think Mythos 5.1 is going to[bring about the AI apocalypse](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/07/anthropic-claude-mythos-ai-hackers-cyberattacks.html) , but there are certainly arguments that it needs stronger guardrails for general use. The U.S. government's temporary export controls made that case pretty clearly. It's also worth noting that Anthropic claims to have deliberately set the guardrails high with a view to reducing the number of false positives in the future after they gather more data.
